lesson.rule: In present-tense sentences, add -s or -es to the verb when the subject is he, she, it, or one person or thing.

lesson.rule: For short adjectives add -er or -est (taller, tallest). For long ones use more or most (more careful). Never use both together.

fragment-subordinate.name: Sentence that starts with 'because' and stops

lesson.rule: A word like because, although, when or if starts an idea that needs a main clause. Join it to one, or add one after it.
lesson.wrong: We stayed inside. Because it was raining.
lesson.right: We stayed inside because it was raining.
lesson.why: A reader who sees 'Because it was raining.' alone is left waiting for the rest of the idea.
lesson.check: Does every sentence that starts with because, although, when or if also say what happened?

comma-splice.name: Two sentences joined by only a comma

lesson.rule: A comma alone cannot join two complete sentences. Use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus and, but or so.

lesson.why: A comma is a small pause, so two full ideas joined by one run together and the reader loses where the first one ends.
lesson.check: Could each side of this comma stand alone as a sentence? If yes, add a joining word or a period.

lesson.check: Is the -s on the noun only? Does the adjective before it stay plain?

lesson.rule: In English, an adjective usually comes before the noun it describes: a red shirt, not a shirt red.
lesson.wrong: She wore a shirt blue.
lesson.why: English readers expect the describing word first, so the usual order lets them picture the thing quickly.
lesson.l1: In Spanish and French, many adjectives come after the noun (casa blanca), but English puts them before.
lesson.check: Does the describing word come right before the noun it describes?

vague-word.name: Vague words: say it more precisely

lesson.rule: Words like thing, stuff, good, bad, nice and really are very broad. Replace each with the exact name, action or detail you mean.
lesson.wrong: Pollution is bad for the ocean.
lesson.right: Pollution harms fish and coral in the ocean.
lesson.why: Exact words give your reader the real picture, and they show your teacher what you know about the topic.
lesson.check: Could I name the exact noun, action or detail instead of this broad word?

practice.prompt: Replace the vague words with exact words.

connector-form.name: Joining words that don't fit together

lesson.rule: Use one joining word per idea. Although/though needs no 'but', because needs no 'so', and 'because of' is followed by a noun, not a full clause.
lesson.wrong: Although it rained, but we played.
lesson.why: Two joining words doing the same job make the sentence confusing, so readers cannot tell which idea matters most.
lesson.l1: In Mandarin, paired words such as 虽然…但是 (although…but) are correct, but English uses only one of them.
lesson.check: Is there one joining word doing the job, or two? And what follows 'because of': a noun or a full clause?

lesson.rule: Some words are often misspelled: because, friend, environment, library, receive, tomorrow. Check them in the word wall or a dictionary.

lesson.rule: English sentences with a describing word need a form of be: I am, he/she/it is, we/you/they are. Write 'She is tired', not 'She tired'.
lesson.wrong: She tired today.
lesson.why: The verb be links the subject to its description, and without it the sentence feels unfinished.
lesson.l1: Arabic and Russian can leave out am, is and are in the present tense, but English always needs one.
lesson.check: Does every describing word after I, he, she, it, we or they have am, is or are before it?
